source.title_on_document: Establishing the importance of co-creation and self-efficacy in creative collaboration with artificial intelligence

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Data and SPSS syntax files are on OSF at https://osf.io/3jqga/ (p. 2; p. 8, Methods; p. 9, Data availability).
supplement.holds: No supplement. The paper says OSF holds the data and syntax files (p. 8; p. 9). The main text prints arm means and SDs (Tables 1 and 2), arm sizes, omnibus ANOVA F tests, post hoc pairwise p-values, and the mediation results (p. 7, Fig. 5). No standard error or confidence interval of any creativity contrast is printed. If the OSF data hold one row per participant, they would allow participant-level two-arm tests.

paper_design_summary: Two online experiments on Prolific randomly assigned adults whose first language is English to write an 8-line poem alone or with a neural poetry generation system. In Study 1 (96 analyzed), participants in the AI arm received a complete AI-generated poem that they could edit (directly or by choosing AI-generated alternative lines), leave as it is, or delete and rewrite (the paper's editor role), and Study 2 (152 analyzed) added a co-creator arm in which the participant and the system wrote alternate lines. Ten professional poets per study rated each poem's creativity on a 1 to 40 scale (Consensual Assessment Technique), and Study 1's rating set also held 50 poems written by the system alone as a benchmark. Participants also rated their own poem's creativity, and Study 2 measured creative self-efficacy as a mediator.

arms.name: Human condition
arms.description: Wrote an 8-line poem (two 4-line stanzas) unassisted; rhyme optional; no time limit.

arms.name: Human-AI condition (editor)
arms.description: Received a complete poem generated by the AI poetry system from a randomly selected set of three topical words. The participant could leave it as it is, edit any line, pick alternative AI-generated lines from a dropdown, or delete the poem and start from scratch, with no time limit. After the participant edits and updates a line, the dropdown offers new alternatives based on it, and alternatives for lines 3 and 4 rhyme with an edited line 1 or 2. The paper calls this the editor role. Role: ideas_supplied (see ai_tool.how_used).

arms.name: AI condition (benchmark, no participants)
arms.description: 50 poems generated entirely by the AI poetry system and added to the expert rating set as a benchmark. No person was assigned to this condition.

participants.exclusions: 101 recruited via Prolific. 6 failed an instrumental attention check and were removed from subsequent analyses, and the paper then reports 'the remaining 96' (48 per arm). 101 − 6 = 95, so the printed counts disagree by one; 96 matches the arm sizes and the 146 rated poems (48 + 48 + 50). The paper does not say whether the 6 were removed before or after random allocation, or from which arm, so no count at assignment is recorded. The 50 AI-condition poems are not people.
participants.who: Prolific participants whose first language is English, with an approval rating of at least 97 percent; mean age 27.23 (SD 8.97), 76 percent female; paid GBP2.50 (about USD3.00).
participants.quote: Participants were 101 individuals recruited via Prolific Academic in exchange for GBP2.50 (approximately USD3.00). Six participants failed to correctly answer an instrumental attention check and were removed from subsequent analyses
participants.locator: p. 2, Results, Study 1; pp. 8-9, Methods (English first language, approval rating, only Study 1 had attention-check failures, n = 6)

ai_tool.name_model: Neural poetry generation system of Van de Cruys (2020): a recurrent neural encoder-decoder trained on 500 million words of CommonCrawl prose (vocabulary of 15 thousand words), with ABAB rhyme and NMF topic constraints and 2048 candidate lines per line. Not a large language model chatbot. Custom web interface built by the authors.
ai_tool.how_used: The system generated a complete 8-line poem from a randomly selected set of three topical words. The participant was told they were free to edit it in a custom interface before submitting: 'You can leave the poem as it is, make only a few minor adjustments, or delete the poem and start from scratch' (p. 3). The interface offered direct edits to any line, a dropdown of alternative AI-generated lines for each line, and new alternatives after the participant edited and updated a line: the dropdown 'updates in real-time based on the newly edited line', and after an edit to line 1 or 2 the alternatives for line 3 or 4 rhyme with it (p. 3; 'Edit line' and 'Update' buttons on every line in Fig. 1, p. 4). The paper reports no data on how many participants edited the poem or how much, so some rated poems may be unedited AI output. AI was available throughout the writing of the rated poem. The codebook has no code for 'AI drafts, the person edits'. The arm combines an AI draft that the study hands to every participant (ideas_supplied) with AI line alternatives that respond to the participant's edits (suggestions). ideas_supplied is recorded because the supplied draft defines the paper's editor role and separates this arm from the Study 2 co-creator arm, which also offers candidate lines and free editing. refinement is the reverse direction (AI edits the person's draft). Review 1 may prefer suggestions, other, or a new code (open_questions).

task.description: Write an 8-line poem of two 4-line stanzas; rhyme optional.

outcomes.name: Expert evaluations of creativity (human-AI vs human)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique: 10 professional poets with published poems (6 with a graduate degree in creative writing, English literature, or a related field; USD40 each) each rated all 146 poems (48 human, 48 human-AI, 50 AI-only) in different, randomly generated orders on a 1 (lowest) to 40 (highest) creativity scale, relative to one another and using the full range, with no information about authors or circumstances. The paper does not state how the 10 ratings were combined per poem and reports no inter-rater reliability. Analysis: one-way ANOVA over the 146 poems in three groups, with post hoc LSD pairwise tests (Table 1 note: t-tests and LSD tests), and the paper states the results for poems. unit is therefore output and n_units counts the 146 poems, the same analysis as S1-O2 and the coding final c010 uses for the same design (S3-O1, S3-O2). Each participant wrote one poem, so the human and human-AI arm means and SDs also describe participants, but the post hoc p-values use an error term that includes the 50 AI-only poems (SD 2.00), which no participant wrote. The printed error df (145) does not match 146 poems (143 expected).

contrasts.reported: Human condition M = 18.23 (SD = 4.94, n = 48) vs human-AI condition M = 12.55 (SD = 4.32, n = 48); post hoc pairwise p < 0.001. Omnibus one-way ANOVA over the three groups of poems, including the 50 AI-only poems: F(2, 145) = 63.48, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.47. No pairwise test statistic or standard error is printed.

outcomes.name: Expert evaluations of creativity (AI-only benchmark poems vs participants' poems)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Same 10-poet CAT ratings and the same one-way ANOVA with post hoc LSD tests as S1-O1. The AI condition is 50 poems that the system generated alone, with no participant, so these contrasts compare AI output with people's output (context, not core). The printed error df (145) does not match 146 poems.

contrasts.reported: AI condition M = 9.45 (SD = 2.00, n = 50 poems) vs human condition M = 18.23 (SD = 4.94, n = 48); post hoc p < 0.001. Same omnibus F(2, 145) = 63.48 as S1-O1.

Human-AI condition M = 12.55 (SD = 4.32, n = 48) vs AI condition M = 9.45 (SD = 2.00, n = 50 poems); post hoc p < 0.001. Poems from people who received AI poems to edit, against AI poems alone, so not an ai_vs_human contrast.

ai_tool.name_model: Same Van de Cruys (2020) recurrent neural poetry generation system as Study 1, in two interfaces: the Study 1 editing interface (human-AI arm) and a redesigned turn-taking interface (co-creator arm).
ai_tool.how_used: Two AI arms with different roles. Human-AI (editor) arm: the system wrote a complete poem that the participant could edit with the Study 1 interface, including AI alternatives based on edited lines, or leave as it is (ideas_supplied, as in Study 1). Co-creator arm: the participant chose a set of three topical words and wrote line 1, the system returned the next line under the ABAB rhyme, and the two alternated until 8 lines, with candidate-line alternatives and free editing of any line at any stage (suggestions). The paper calls this process 'akin to a conversation'. One study-level code cannot cover both arms, so the role is other. AI was available while the rated poem was written in both arms.

task.description: Write an 8-line poem of two 4-line stanzas (same procedure as Study 1).
task.duration: No time limit: Study 2 followed the same procedure as Study 1, which imposed none. Study 2 states no limit of its own.

outcomes.name: Expert evaluations of creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: CAT ratings from 10 different professional poets (USD40 each) on the 1 to 40 scale, as in Study 1. Aggregation across poets and inter-rater reliability are not reported. One-way ANOVA with post hoc LSD pairwise tests (Table 2 note). One poem per participant: the error df (149) equals 152 participants minus 3 arms, so one row is one participant. Fig. 4 shows the arm means with 95% CI error bars and labels two differences. PROCESS Model 4 mediation through creative self-efficacy (10,000 bootstrap samples, bias-corrected 95% CIs) is reported for two pairs of arms, and its numbers sit in those contrasts.

Fig. 4 labels the difference Δ = 3.21**. Omnibus one-way ANOVA across the three arms: F(2, 149) = 5.77, p = 0.004, partial η2 = 0.07.

eligibility.reason: Both studies randomly assign individual Prolific participants to write a poem alone or with an AI poetry generator (p. 2; p. 4; p. 9: 'Condition assignments were random in both studies'). Study 1 analyzed 96 people (48 + 48; the printed 101 recruited minus 6 excluded would give 95) and Study 2 analyzed 152 (51 + 50 + 51), so both exceed 50. The outcome is ten professional poets' Consensual Assessment Technique rating of each poem's creativity (1 to 40), and the AI was available while the AI-arm poems were written. Editing the AI poem was optional (p. 3), which does not affect criterion 1, because the study randomized access to the AI poem and its tools. Study 1's 50 AI-only poems give AI-versus-human context (S1-O2) and do not count toward the 50, and the self-rated creativity outcomes (S1-O3, S2-O2) fail criterion 3. Neither changes eligibility. Scope flag for Review 1: the AI is a recurrent neural encoder-decoder poetry generator (Van de Cruys 2020), not a large language model. It generates text from topic words and the participant's lines, and the paper calls it a generative AI system, so it fits the codebook's definition.

one_line_finding: Professional poets rated poems submitted by people who received an AI-generated poem to edit as less creative than poems written alone (Study 1: 12.55 vs 18.23 on a 1 to 40 scale, p < 0.001, p. 4 and Table 1; Study 2: 12.53 vs 15.74, p = 0.001, p. 6 and Table 2 on p. 7), while writing line by line in turns with the AI did not differ from writing alone (14.70 vs 15.74, p = 0.278) and scored higher than the editing condition (p = 0.026).
open_questions: Scope: is the Van de Cruys (2020) recurrent neural poetry generator within the codebook's definition of generative AI? It is a neural text generator, not a large language model. It produces lines from topic words and the participant's lines, and the paper calls it 'a generative AI system' (p. 2).

AI role: the codebook has no code for 'AI drafts the whole output, the person edits'. The editor arm is coded ideas_supplied for the AI poem that the study hands every participant. The participant's edits also drive the AI: after a participant edits and updates a line, the dropdown offers new AI lines based on it (p. 3; Fig. 1, p. 4). Review 1 may prefer suggestions, other, or a new code. Study 2's study-level role is other, with each arm's role in how_used.

Study 1 counts disagree. 101 recruited minus 6 excluded is 95, but the paper reports 96 remaining (48 + 48), and the omnibus ANOVA prints F(2, 145) although 146 poems in three groups give an error df of 143 (p. 2; p. 4). One printed count or the df is wrong, and the OSF data would settle it.
Study 1: the paper does not say whether the 6 attention-check failures were removed before or after random allocation, or from which arm (p. 2; p. 9).

Study 2 expert-creativity SD for the human condition: the text prints 9.24 (p. 6) and Table 2 prints 4.98 (p. 7). 9.24 is the same arm's self-reported creativity SD. Fig. 4's 95% CI error bar for the human arm spans about 14.3 to 17.2 by visual reading (the ends are not printed), a half-width near 1.4 with n = 51, which fits an SD near 5 and not 9.24 (half-width near 2.6). Extraction should use 4.98 unless the OSF data say otherwise. The printed F(2, 149) = 5.77 and post hoc p-values reproduce, to rounding, from Table 2 with 4.98 (p = 0.001, 0.026, 0.28) but not with 9.24 (F = 3.09). This is checker and finalizer arithmetic, not a printed value.

Study 1 post hoc p-values come from a three-group ANOVA over 146 poems whose error term includes the 50 AI-only poems (SD 2.00), so they are not two-arm tests, and S1-O1's unit is output for that reason. No standard error of any creativity contrast is printed in either study. Effects and standard errors should come from the arm means, SDs, and sizes, or from the OSF data.

Primary record for Study 2's ai_vs_bau question: two AI arms share the human arm, and neither is free chatbot use (codebook section 8, rule 3). The paper calls the co-creator process 'akin to a conversation' (p. 5), which may make it the closer arm. The paper's own hypothesis is the co-creator vs editor contrast (ai_design).
Study 2 does not print the number of poems rated. The arm sizes (51 + 50 + 51) and the error df of F(2, 149) imply one poem per participant, 152 in all.

Editing was optional in the editor arms. The instructions said 'You can leave the poem as it is' (p. 3), and Study 2 followed the same procedure (p. 5). The paper reports no data on how many participants changed the AI poem or how much, so some rated human-AI poems may be unedited AI output. If the OSF data hold the submitted poems and the system's drafts, they would show this.

Both studies: the paper does not say how the 10 poets' ratings were combined into one score per poem, and it reports no inter-rater reliability (pp. 3-5). The arm means and SDs describe that unstated score. The OSF data may hold the separate ratings.
notes: Outcomes S1-O3 and S2-O2 are self-ratings of the participant's own poem, listed for completeness. They are not scored on the output and do not count toward eligibility. Creative self-efficacy (Study 2: three-item Tierney and Farmer scale, alpha = 0.92, 1 to 7; human 4.71 (SD 1.45), co-creator 4.62 (SD 1.43), human-AI 3.74 (SD 1.43); F(2, 149) = 7.01, p = 0.001, partial eta2 = 0.09; p. 5, Fig. 3 on p. 6, Table 2 on p. 7) is a self-reported mediator and is not listed as an outcome. No diversity outcome and no outcome produced after AI was removed. statistics_available lists what the paper prints for the contrast or either of its arms. The pairwise post hoc tests print only p, so the omnibus F tests (df1 = 2) stay in 'reported'. Each participant wrote one poem. S1-O1 and S1-O2 use unit output (n_units 146), because the paper's Study 1 analysis is one ANOVA over 146 poems, 50 of them AI-only poems with no participant, as final c010 codes the same design. S2-O1, S1-O3, and S2-O2 use unit participant, because their analyses have one row per participant. The paper states 'All conditions, measures and exclusions are reported' (p. 2) and mentions no preregistration. Studies 1 and 2 recruited separately on Prolific, and the paper does not say whether one person could take part in both. Holzner et al. (2025) lists this paper as HAI10 and CP03 (candidates.json lead, not checked against that paper). This form was reconciled on 2026-10-05 from the raw forms dated October 5. It replaces the October 4 reconciled file, which was built from an earlier pair of raw forms. Finalized on 2026-10-05 from three challenge files. The assignment and outcome checkers raised four problems, and all four are corrected (see final). The people checker raised none and confirmed every count. The finalizer also changed source.supplement.holds to say that the paper, not this form, describes the OSF contents, and changed 'analyzes' to 'analyzed' in eligibility.reason, following the spec.

differences.a: refinement (A's how_used says the codebook roles fit poorly and that the closest are ideas_supplied or other)
differences.resolved: ideas_supplied (neither form). The codebook defines refinement as AI that edits or comments on the person's own draft. Here the person edits the AI's poem, the reverse direction. The study hands each participant a complete AI-generated poem before any writing, and the participant never prompts the AI, which is the defining feature of ideas_supplied, the closest code. The dropdown of alternative AI lines is recorded in how_used, and open_questions asks Review 1 whether 'AI drafts, person edits' needs its own code.
differences.quote: they were also told that they will first be provided with a poem produced by an algorithm ... and that they can edit the poem as freely as they wish before submitting it
differences.locator: p. 3, Results, Study 1 (instructions to the human-AI condition)

differences.a: suggestions (A's how_used notes that the roles differ by arm)
differences.resolved: other (B). Study 2 has two AI arms with different roles. The editor arm receives a finished AI poem to edit (ideas_supplied, as in Study 1). The co-creator arm writes alternate lines with the system (suggestions). One study-level code cannot describe both arms, so the role is other, and each arm's role is in how_used and in the arm descriptions. Reconciled c056 used other when no single code fit.

The S1 editor-arm description and open question 2 now give Review 1 the evidence and the alternatives (suggestions, other, or a new code). The reconciliation entry for studies[S1].ai_tool.role stays unchanged as a record, and its 'never prompts' reason no longer holds. Criterion 1 is unaffected.

open_items.item: Generative-AI scope (open question 1): the tool is the Van de Cruys (2020) recurrent neural encoder-decoder poetry generator, not a large language model. It produces text from topic words and from the participant's lines, and the paper calls it 'a generative AI system' (p. 2), so it fits codebook section 1 as written and criterion 1 is met. If Review 1 reads section 1 as requiring a large language model, criterion 1 fails in both studies and the paper leaves the core. The paper describes the architecture (p. 3), so no other source is needed. The decision is Review 1's.

Role code for the editor arms (open question 2): ideas_supplied is recorded, and Review 1 may prefer suggestions, other, or a new code, because the participant's edits also drive new AI lines (p. 3; Fig. 1, p. 4). The paper describes the interface fully. No criterion depends on the role code.

Study 1 counts (open question 3): 101 recruited minus 6 excluded is 95, but the paper prints 96 remaining (48 + 48), and the ANOVA prints error df 145 where 146 poems give 143. Rebuilt from Table 1, the printed F = 63.48 matches neither df (62.30 at 143; arithmetic, not printed). Either people count exceeds 50.

Study 1 exclusions (open question 4): the paper does not say whether the 6 attention-check failures were removed before or after allocation, or from which arm, so n_randomized stays null. The OSF data may keep the six with their condition. If not, only the authors can say. Criterion 2 counts people analyzed (96).

Study 2 human-arm SD for expert creativity (open question 5): the text prints 9.24 and Table 2 prints 4.98. The printed F(2, 149) = 5.77 and post hoc p-values reproduce from Table 2 with 4.98 but not with 9.24 (F = 3.09), and the Fig. 4 error bar fits 4.98. Extraction uses 4.98.

Study 1 inference (open question 6): the post hoc p-values use an error term that includes the 50 AI-only poems, and neither study prints a standard error for a creativity contrast. The printed arm means, SDs, and sizes give d and SE(d) by the codebook section 10 formula, at the participant level because each participant wrote one poem.

Primary record for Study 2's ai_vs_bau question (open question 7): two AI arms share the human arm. Review 1 applies codebook section 8, rule 3, to facts the form already records (the paper calls the co-creator process 'akin to a conversation', p. 5).
Study 2 poem count (open question 8): not printed, but the arm sizes (51 + 50 + 51) and the error df of F(2, 149) fix one poem per participant, 152 in all.

Editing extent (open question 9, new): editing the AI poem was optional (p. 3), and the paper reports no data on how many editor-arm participants changed it or how much. The randomized contrast does not depend on it. The OSF data may hold the submitted poems and the system's drafts.

Rating aggregation (open question 10, new): the paper does not say how the 10 poets' ratings were combined per poem and reports no inter-rater reliability. The OSF data may hold the separate ratings. If not, the authors can say.
